# A module that looks somewhere {#sec-directional-om}

@sec-axial-source compressed the source and left the kernel alone. It left one
thing alone that it should not have: the module. Every scattered photon in that
chapter was accepted as if it had arrived along the line from the source
centroid,

```python
angular = self.detector.angular_weight(elements.centroid_m)   # one scalar per OM
scale_area = self.detector.effective_area_m2 * angular
```

and the metadata said so plainly --- *"source-centroid direction for all axial
components; exact arbitrary directional-OM axial transport is not yet
implemented"*. This chapter implements it.

The reason it was left is worth stating before the fix, because it is the whole
difficulty. A problem with **one** preferred direction separates: a directed
flash read by an isotropic detector, or an isotropic flash read by a directed
detector, are both a single sum over multipoles $M_l(r)$, and they are the
*same* $M_l$. A real event is directed and a real module looks somewhere, so
there are two preferred directions at once, and the integral over the direction
of $\mathbf k$ no longer collapses by Gegenbauer's theorem. What replaces it is
an exact factorisation, not an expansion in anything small.

Nothing here changes the medium ($g=0.9$ Henyey--Greenstein), the Fourier
convention $e^{+i\omega t}$, the two-field spectral source, or the existing
normalisations. The isotropic path is bit-for-bit what it was.

## What the module actually sees {#sec-directional-what}

A module with acceptance $A$ and axis $\hat n$ measures

$$R(\mathbf r)=\int d\hat s\;A(\hat s\cdot\hat n)\,I(\mathbf r,\hat s),$$

an integral over the *arrival* direction. The centroid approximation replaces
$A(\hat s\cdot\hat n)$ by its value at one $\hat s$. For unscattered light that
is nearly right, because the arrival direction really is nearly the line to the
emitting element --- and even there it is not exactly right, since a Cherenkov
cone photon leaves from a point along the chord and not from the centroid. For
scattered light it is not right at all: the arrival direction has a
distribution, and that distribution depends on distance and on frequency.

## Conventions {#sec-directional-conventions}

Real orthonormal harmonics $\tilde Y_{lm}$ throughout the code, the ones
`event_moments.real_spherical_harmonics` and its fused twin
`axial_fast._harmonics_into` already build; complex $Y_{lm}$ with the
Condon--Shortley phase in the derivation, converted once. Normalised Legendre
$p_l=\sqrt{(2l+1)/2}\,P_l$ as in `angular.py`. Acceptance coefficients
$\alpha_\lambda=2\pi\int A P_\lambda\,dx$, so an isotropic module of unit
efficiency has $\alpha_0=4\pi$ and nothing else --- exactly
`cache.acceptance_coefficients`.

One sign is fixed once and never again. `DetectorArray.orientations` points
*towards* the source, so a photon travelling along $\hat s$ arrives head-on
when $\hat s=-\,$`orientation`. The derivation uses the *viewing* direction
$\hat n=-\,$`orientation`, and the conversion happens on one line of
`transport._transport_directional`.

$L$ is the scattering truncation, $L_s$ the source degree, $M$ the source
azimuthal degree, $L_A$ the **acceptance bandwidth** --- and $L_A$ is measured,
not assumed (@sec-directional-bandwidth).

## The azimuthal blocks {#sec-directional-blocks}

In $k$-space, for each $\mathbf k$, put the polar axis along $\hat k$. Streaming
is then multiplication by $\mu=\hat s\cdot\hat k$ and Henyey--Greenstein is
diagonal in $(l,m)$, so both operators are diagonal in $m$ and the angular
system splits:

$$(d_0-\gamma_l)h_{lm}+ik\,a_{lm}h_{l-1,m}+ik\,a_{l+1,m}h_{l+1,m}=A_{lm},
\qquad a_{lm}=\sqrt{\frac{l^2-m^2}{4l^2-1}},$$

for $l\ge|m|$, with $\gamma_l=\sigma_s g^l$ up to $L$ and zero above. Three
properties follow and all three are used.

**The block begins at $l=|m|$.** The coupling downwards vanishes by itself,
$a_{|m|,m}=0$, so the system has $L-|m|+1$ rows rather than $L+1$.

**The matrix is complex symmetric**, $A_{l,l-1}=A_{l-1,l}=ik\,a_{lm}$. Its
resolvent is therefore symmetric, $G^{(m)}_{\lambda l}=G^{(m)}_{l\lambda}$: one
solve serves the source index and the detector index alike. This is the sense
in which `angular.py` was always computing an *adjoint* Green coefficient ---
today's $h_l$ is the zeroth column of the $m=0$ block, and equally its zeroth
row.

**$G^{(m)}=G^{(-m)}$**, because $a_{lm}$ depends on $m^2$. That is a derivation,
not a convention, and it is what lets the sum over $\pm\nu$ fold in
@sec-directional-inversion.

Orders of scattering split as before: with $\Gamma=\operatorname{diag}\gamma_l$,
$G_0$ the free resolvent and $G$ the full one,

$$\text{first}=G_0\Gamma G_0,\qquad
\text{$\ge 2$}=G\Gamma G_0\Gamma G_0=G-G_0-G_0\Gamma G_0,$$

and the right-hand form shows the second operator is symmetric too, being a
difference of symmetric ones.

## The free tail, without dividing two underflows {#sec-directional-tail}

Above $L$ the right-hand side vanishes and the recurrence is homogeneous. With
$z=i d_0/k$,

$$a_{l+1,m}y_{l+1}=z\,y_l-a_{lm}y_{l-1},$$

which is the three-term recurrence of associated Legendre functions in degree.
Its two solutions are the normalised $\hat P_{lm}(z)$, which grows, and
$\hat Q_{lm}(z)$, which decays; the physical one is the minimal solution, and at
$m=0$ it is exactly what `angular.py` already computes, since
$\int_{-1}^{1}P_l(\mu)\,d\mu/(d_0+ik\mu)=-2Q_l(z)/(ik)$.

The ratio $R^{(m)}_l=\hat Q_{l+1,m}/\hat Q_{lm}$ obeys the downward continued
fraction

$$R^{(m)}_{l-1}=\frac{a_{lm}}{z-a_{l+1,m}R^{(m)}_{l}},$$

and here is why the branch needs no choosing. Asymptotically $a_{lm}\to 1/2$ and
the recurrence degenerates to $y_{l+1}-2zy_l+y_{l-1}=0$ with roots
$\rho^{\pm1}$, $|\rho|<1$. Iterated *downwards*, the map above has the minimal
solution as its attracting fixed point (Pincherle), so any seed at depth $D$
leaves an error of order $|\rho|^{2(D-l)}$ and the decaying solution is selected
by the direction of the iteration. `tail_ratios_continued_fraction` does exactly
this, with the depth taken from the measured $\eta=-\ln|\rho|$.

That alone is enough but not fast enough: at large $k$, $\eta\approx\sigma_t/k$
and the needed depth runs into thousands of steps per node. The existing $m=0$
code avoids it by a forward recurrence from the closed form
$m_0=2\arctan(k/d_0)/k$; for $m\ne0$ there is no closed form. Instead we raise
$m$ exactly. The associated-Legendre relation

$$X_l^{m+1}(z)=(z^2-1)^{-1/2}\bigl[(l-m)zX_l^m(z)-(l+m)X_{l-1}^m(z)\bigr]$$

holds for both kinds, so it maps the minimal solution to the minimal solution.
Written purely in ratios --- which is the point ---

$$v^{(m)}_l=(l-m)z-(l+m)\,b_l\big/R^{(m)}_{l-1},\qquad
b_l=\sqrt{\frac{(2l+1)(l-m)}{(2l-1)(l+m)}},$$

$$R^{(m+1)}_l=\sqrt{\frac{(l-m)(l+m+1)}{(l+1-m)(l+m+2)}}\;
\frac{v^{(m)}_{l+1}}{v^{(m)}_l}\;R^{(m)}_l .$$

Ratios go in and ratios come out; nothing underflowing is ever divided by
anything underflowing, and $(z^2-1)^{-1/2}$ cancels and is never formed, so no
branch of a square root enters. A zero of $\hat Q_{l,m+1}$ would make $v$ small;
`free_tail_ratios_m` measures $|v|$ against the larger of its two terms and
falls back to the continued fraction on those nodes, reporting how many.

**Measured.** Against a continued fraction run to depth $40\,000$, over
$k\in[0.02,8]\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ (that is $|\rho|$ from $0.35$ to $0.994$) and
$\omega\in\{0,0.15\}$: worst relative difference $1.5\times10^{-14}$ for
$m=1,2,3$, with **zero** fallback nodes. The selection of the decaying branch
is checked separately by closing the recurrence on the returned ratios: residual
$10^{-12}$, and the solution decays.

## The module fixes the output degree {#sec-directional-bandwidth}

Expanding $A$ and using the addition theorem,

$$\int d\hat s\,A(\hat s\cdot\hat n)\tilde I(\mathbf k,\hat s)
=\sum_{\lambda\le L_A}\alpha_\lambda\sum_{\nu}
 Y_{\lambda\nu}\bigl(\hat n^{(k)}\bigr)h_{\lambda\nu}(\mathbf k).$$

Two consequences carry the whole cost argument. The **output** degree is bounded
by the acceptance bandwidth, not by the source degree: only $L_A+1$ rows of the
resolvent are needed. And only blocks with $|\nu|\le L_A$ appear, because
$|\nu|\le\lambda$. For a cubic module that is four distinct blocks and ten pairs
$(\lambda,|\nu|)$ instead of one.

Whether a module response really is cubic is a question about the data, and
`directional.acceptance_bandwidth` answers it by measurement: it returns the
largest degree above tolerance and the largest coefficient above that degree.
A response of the form $\max(\text{polynomial},0)$ whose polynomial dips below
zero inside $[-1,1]$ is **not** band-limited --- the clip puts a kink in it and
the coefficients decay only algebraically. In that case the measured bandwidth
runs into the probe range, and `TransportKernel.acceptance` refuses rather than
truncating silently; `KernelConfig.acceptance_degree` accepts a truncation
explicitly and the reported residual says how big a one.

## The integral over $\hat k$ {#sec-directional-inversion}

This is the part that does not separate. The source moments and the module axis
both have to be expressed in each $\hat k$ frame, so the integrand depends on
$\hat k$ through two rotated objects.

Write both rotations as Wigner $D$ matrices and use the Clebsch--Gordan series
on the product; $D^J_{M0}(R_k)=\sqrt{4\pi/(2J+1)}\,Y^*_{JM}(\hat k)$ collapses
the whole $\hat k$ dependence onto a **single** harmonic of degree
$J\in[\,|l-\lambda|,\,l+\lambda\,]$, and the familiar
$\int d\hat k\,e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}Y^*_{JM}(\hat k)
=4\pi i^J j_J(kr)Y^*_{JM}(\hat r)$ finishes it.

Two things then happen that decide the cost. The sum over the block index $\nu$
**factorises out of the geometry**, because the Clebsch--Gordan coefficient
carrying the magnetic indices does not depend on $\nu$:

$$g_{\lambda lJ}(k,\omega)=\sum_\nu(-1)^\nu
\langle\lambda\nu;l,-\nu|J0\rangle\,G^{(\nu)}_{\lambda l}(k,\omega),$$

one scalar per *triple*, not per quadruple. And a **parity rule** appears: from
$\langle\lambda,-\nu;l,\nu|J0\rangle=(-1)^{\lambda+l-J}
\langle\lambda\nu;l,-\nu|J0\rangle$ together with $G^{(\nu)}=G^{(-\nu)}$, the
folded sum vanishes unless $l+\lambda+J$ is even. Measured directly on the
coefficients: the largest odd-parity value is $2.2\times10^{-16}$. It is a
property of the algebra, not a filter imposed on it.

Finally, take the polar axis along $\hat r$. Then $Y^*_{JM}(\hat r)\propto
\delta_{M0}$, the double sum over magnetic indices collapses to one, and with

$$t_{l\lambda\mu}(r,\omega)=\frac{1}{2\pi^2}\sum_J i^J
(-1)^\mu\langle\lambda\mu;l,-\mu|J0\rangle
\int k^2 j_J(kr)\,g_{\lambda lJ}(k,\omega)\,dk$$

the response is

$$\boxed{\;R(\mathbf r)=\sum_{l\le L_s}\sum_{\lambda\le L_A}
\sum_{|\mu|\le\min(l,\lambda)}
\alpha_\lambda\,t_{l\lambda|\mu|}(r,\omega)\,
\tilde Y_{\lambda\mu}\bigl(\hat n^{(\hat r)}\bigr)\,
\tilde S_{l\mu}^{(\hat r)}(\omega)\;}$$

with every harmonic in the frame whose polar axis is $\hat r$. The azimuth of
that frame is arbitrary: only the difference of the source and module azimuths
enters, which is why $t$ depends on $|\mu|$ and the whole apply stays in real
arithmetic apart from the frequency phase.

### Where the old cache sits inside the new one {#sec-directional-containment}

Set $\lambda=0$: then $\nu=0$ and $J=l$, and $t_{l00}=M_l/\sqrt{2l+1}$ --- the
present cache for a directed source and an isotropic module. Set $l=0$: then
$\mu=0$ and $J=\lambda$, and the same array reappears for an isotropic flash and
a directed module. Today's code uses one array for both cases; that is not a
coincidence but $G^{(0)}_{0l}=G^{(0)}_{l0}$. The new table contains the old one
as its two boundary rows, and the test asserting it agrees to
$2\times10^{-15}$ is the first thing that runs.

## Two references, at two distances {#sec-directional-references}

| | what it shares with production | what it replaces |
|---|---|---|
| `khat_quadrature_response` | the $m$-block solve | the Clebsch--Gordan contraction, the parity rule, the $\hat r$-frame collapse --- all replaced by an explicit numerical integral over $\hat k$ with the rotations done by hand at each node |
| `dense_angular_reference` | nothing but the physics | the blocks as well: it builds $\langle Y_{lm}|\hat s|Y_{l'm'}\rangle$ by quadrature, assembles the full lab-frame matrix for every $(k,\hat k)$ and inverts it |
| `axisymmetric_reference` | the $m$-block solve | the geometry: source axis, module axis and displacement on one line, so the azimuthal integral is exactly $2\pi$ |

The third deserves a remark, because it is the one that is easy to get wrong.
Even when the whole geometry is axisymmetric, the blocks $\nu\ne0$ still
contribute --- the polar axis of each node frame is $\hat k$, not the symmetry
axis. A reference that dropped them would agree with a production path that
dropped them too, and the test would prove nothing.

**Measured.** Production against the $\hat k$ quadrature:
$5.9\times10^{-16}$ at $\omega=0$ and $1.5\times10^{-14}$ at $\omega=0.07$.
The two references against each other, as the dense truncation degree rises:

| dense degree | $\omega=0$ | $\omega=0.08$ |
|---:|---|---|
| 4 | $6.2\times10^{-4}$ | $1.3\times10^{-4}$ |
| 8 | $1.4\times10^{-7}$ | $4.4\times10^{-9}$ |
| 12 | $5.9\times10^{-11}$ | $3.5\times10^{-13}$ |

The residual at degree 4 is the dense route's own hard truncation --- it has no
tail closure --- and it converges away, which is the statement that the closure
is right.

## Every formula, and where it lives {#sec-directional-map}

| formula | function or class |
|---|---|
| $a_{lm}$ | `angular.coupling_coefficients` |
| the block system, Schur-closed | `angular.solve_tail_system_m` |
| continued fraction (CF) | `angular.tail_ratios_continued_fraction` |
| raising in $m$, with the guard | `angular.free_tail_ratios_m` |
| $G^{(m)}_{\lambda l}$, orders 1 and $\ge2$ | `angular.resolvent_rows` |
| dense block, no closure | `angular.dense_block_reference` |
| $\alpha_\lambda$, and measuring $L_A$ | `cache.acceptance_coefficients`, `directional.acceptance_bandwidth` |
| $\langle\cdot\rangle$, parity, $(\lambda,l,J)$ and $(\lambda,|\mu|)$ tables | `directional.CouplingTable` |
| $g_{\lambda lJ}\to M_{\lambda lJ}\to t_{l\lambda\mu}$ | `directional.DirectionalCache.build` |
| radial lookup, detrended and phase-corrected | `directional.DirectionalCache.coefficients_at` |
| $d^l_{\mu\nu}(\theta)$ | `directional.wigner_small_d` |
| $E^l_{\nu\mu}$, complex construction | `directional.real_rotation_rows` |
| $E^l_{\nu\mu}$, the real arithmetic the kernel performs | `directional.rotation_rows_explicit` |
| the boxed formula, numpy | `directional.directional_response` |
| the boxed formula, fused | `_directional_numba.PreparedDirectionalKernel.apply` |
| unscattered light, exact arrival direction | `ballistic.ballistic_directional`, `ballistic_fast.ballistic_directional_fast` |
| production entry point | `transport.TransportKernel._transport_directional` |
| references | `experimental.directional_reference` |

## Complexity and memory {#sec-directional-cost}

Counting at $L_s=32$, $M=4$, $L_A=3$, $L=24$:

| object | $m=0$ route | directional route | factor |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| distinct angular blocks | 1 | 4 | 4 |
| right-hand sides per block | 1 | $L_A+1-|m|$ | 10 in total |
| cached numbers per degree | 1 | 10 | 10 |
| $(\lambda,l,J)$ triples | 33 | 320 | 9.7 |
| harmonics per (cell, receiver) | $\mathcal O(L_sM)$ | $+\;d^l_{\nu\mu}$, $(2L_A{+}1)(M{+}1)$ per $l$ | --- |

The parity rule is what keeps the cache at ten numbers per degree rather than
sixteen; it is applied when $M_{\lambda lJ}$ is folded into $t_{l\lambda\mu}$,
so the stored array never carries the odd triples at all.

At the production grid --- 220 radii, 41 frequencies, 2000 $k$ nodes --- the
stored table is $(41,220,33,10,2)$ complex, $95.3$ MB per wavelength against
$9.5$ MB for the $m=0$ cache. The prepared spline used by the fused kernel is
four cubic coefficients per interval, about $4\times$ that again, so the
production loop builds it one wavelength at a time and discards it rather than
holding nine.

## Measured {#sec-directional-measured}

Machine: two cores, 7 GB, numpy 2.4.4, scipy 1.17.1, **no numba** (no route to
PyPI from that machine), so the table below times the numpy path only. The
fused kernels were compiled and measured separately, on the author's machine,
and those numbers are in @sec-directional-numba-measured; the numpy path is
what the fused kernel is asserted equal to in
`tests/test_directional_numba.py`. `scripts/benchmark_directional.py` runs
every stage on whichever backends are present and labels each pair with both.

Settings: $L=24$, $L_s=32$, $M=4$, $L_A=3$, $k_{\max}=8\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ with
2000 nodes, 220 radii from 3 to 300 m, 41 frequencies.

| stage | $m=0$ route | directional | factor | target |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| angular solve, 41 frequencies | $0.375\,\mathrm s$ | $2.949\,\mathrm s$ | $7.9\times$ | $\approx 8\times$ |
| cache build, one wavelength | $7.45\,\mathrm s$ | $17.00\,\mathrm s$ | $2.3\times$ | --- |
| cache size, one wavelength | $9.53\,\mathrm{MB}$ | $95.3\,\mathrm{MB}$ | $10.0\times$ | $\le 16\times$ |
| apply, numpy, per module | $0.129\,\mathrm s$ | $0.836\,\mathrm s$ | $6.5\times$ | $\approx 10\times$ |

Peak RSS: $538$ MiB for the cache build, $2.37$ GiB for the numpy apply on
eight modules (the dominant term there is the prepared spline of the cache, not
the kernel). The apply row is 372 source cells and 41 frequencies per module.

### With numba, on the author's machine {#sec-directional-numba-measured}

The numbers above are numpy against numpy. Compiled, and at production size:

| quantity | measured |
|---|---:|
| directional apply, numba against numpy | $\approx 22\times$ faster |
| directional apply against the $m=0$ apply, both numba | $\approx 9.8\times$ |
| fused kernel against its numpy twin | $7.5\times10^{-15}$ relative |
| full suite | 322 passed, including real G4 files |
| $m$-block and fused-kernel tests | 46 passed |
| BGVD module response | $L_A=3$, clip inactive, residual $3.4\times10^{-14}$ |
| joint rotation, 2304 modules | $1.4\times10^{-14}$ |
| turning the modules over, 2304 modules | signal changes by $\approx95\%$ |

The second row is the one that matters and the one that is easy to get wrong.
An early version of `scripts/benchmark_directional.py` timed the *fused*
directional apply against the *numpy* $m=0$ route and so appeared to show the
new method beating the old one, which it does not and cannot: it was measuring
a compiler against an interpreter and calling the difference physics. The
script now names both backends of every pair it reports and never mixes them.

Source compilation is untouched --- the same compiler, the same lattice, the
same channels --- and measured at $0.107\,\mathrm s$ for 372 cells and 277
channels with the numpy compiler.

One number is worth keeping, because it was the entire bottleneck at first.
Built naively, with the Bessel table rebuilt inside the frequency loop, the
directional cache took $147\,\mathrm s$ of which $133\,\mathrm s$ was
`spherical_jn`: a $20\times$ factor that had nothing to do with the physics.
Hoisting the table out --- the same thing `ResponseCache.build` already did ---
left $17\,\mathrm s$, of which $11.2\,\mathrm s$ is the contraction and
$2.9\,\mathrm s$ the angular solve. The lesson generalises: the new route adds
indices to the contraction, so anything that was previously amortised over
frequencies has to stay amortised.

## What is still approximate {#sec-directional-remaining}

* the source lattice: cells of `cell_m` along the axis and across it, and the
  azimuthal truncation at $M$ --- unchanged from @sec-axial-source, and
  unchanged by this chapter;
* the acceptance is band-limited at $L_A$. For a genuinely cubic module this is
  exact; for a clipped one it is a truncation, and the code refuses to make it
  silently;
* the two-field spectral source and the cone frozen at the reference phase
  index --- unchanged;
* the radial interpolation of the cache, now over ten numbers per degree rather
  than one; the interpolation rule and grid are identical, so its error is the
  same error;
* the scattered orders stop at "first" and "two or more", as before.

Not approximate any more: the module response for the scattered orders, and the
arrival direction of unscattered light, which is now the exact direction from
each element's cone root rather than the line to the centroid.

## Running it {#sec-directional-running}

```bash
python scripts/probe_bipolar_identity.py --output .build/review/directional
python scripts/benchmark_directional.py --output .build/review/directional
python -m pytest -q tests/test_angular_m_blocks.py tests/test_directional.py \
                   tests/test_directional_numba.py
# private inputs stay on the machine that holds them
python scripts/smoke_bgvd_directional.py --bgvd <path to bgvd-model> \
       --output .build/review/bgvd-directional
```

A method name says how the **source** is handled --- `isotropic`, `track`,
`axial` --- and the module model is a property of the module, resolved from its
measured acceptance bandwidth. `kernel.transport(source)` therefore uses the
exact kernel whenever the module is directional and the old engine when it is
not, and the result says which: `metadata["detector_angular_model"]` is
`exact_m_blocks` for the former. `method="directional"` forces the exact model
even for an isotropic module, and the superseded source-centroid model survives
as the experimental `axial_centroid` / `track_centroid` for regression only.

`build()` makes the tables that choice will read and no others ---
`kernel.cache_kinds(method)` says which, and `build(source=...)` resolves both
the table and the wavelengths from the source rather than guessing. Building
the multipole tables and then transporting through the directional kernel was
doing the expensive half of the work twice; building the wavelength quadrature
for a monochromatic flash, which reads one line, was doing it for nothing.
